fields.explanation: An ORM (Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM, ActiveRecord) maps table rows to objects and writes the SQL for you, so queries live in the host language instead of in SQL strings. It does not replace the database engine, and it does not make queries fast: a loop that touches a relation per row is the classic N+1. Schema changes still need migrations.

evidence: knowledge: ActiveRecord is Ruby and dynamically typed; typed query results are a property of Prisma and Drizzle in TypeScript, not of ORMs in general
notes: Hint survives because options 1 and 2 both mention generated SQL, so it matches no single option.

fields.hint: Ask what else the browser was going to do with that thread during those 600 ms.
fields.explanation: The main thread runs script, style, layout, paint and event handlers, so a task that holds it for hundreds of milliseconds delays the paint that answers a click or a keystroke — that delay is what INP measures. Clicks and keystrokes are dispatched on the main thread, so the browser can only respond once the task yields, which is why long work is split or moved to a worker. Network transfers continue in the background, so throughput is not what suffers.

problems: hint states the rule the item tests (script, layout, paint and event handling share one thread), which is what makes the key right and the 'another thread' distractor wrong
explanation's blanket claim that input is not handled on a separate thread is too broad: composited scrolling is handled off the main thread
evidence: https://web.dev/articles/vitals — INP measures interactivity; good INP is 200 ms or less
knowledge: event dispatch for clicks and keystrokes runs on the main thread, while scroll can be composited off it
notes: Key, stem duration and the three distractors are sound; both fixes are local.

fields.hint: Ask what each of these resources still costs the device after the bytes have arrived.
fields.explanation: JavaScript is the only item on this list that is parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread after it arrives, so it delays first paint and the first interaction as well as the download; code the page never ships costs nothing at any of those stages. A closer edge, smaller CSS and better image encoding reduce transfer time only. Measure before choosing: web.dev's guideline breakdown for a well-optimized page puts about 40% of LCP in TTFB and about 40% in loading the LCP resource, so on an image-led page the image work comes first.

fields.question: A function returns a list of active users. Which assertion survives an unrelated change to the user record and still fails when the wrong users come back?
fields.explanation: Assert what the function promises — which users are active — and leave the rest alone. Pinning every field breaks whenever an unrelated field is added, and asserting a length passes when the wrong three come back. A truthy check survives every change because it can never fail, which is survival without information.

problems: multiple-defensible: 'The result is truthy' survives any unrelated change without ever becoming wrong, so it answers the original stem ('most likely to survive an unrelated change without becoming wrong') at least as well as the key
evidence: node: [] and [{id:1}] are both truthy, so a truthy assertion cannot become wrong under any change; a hard-coded full-object array breaks as soon as a field is added
notes: Stem now carries both requirements (survives an unrelated change, still fails on wrong users) so only option 1 satisfies them; explanation extended to dismiss the truthy option.

fields.hint: Ask which inputs could catch a bug that every other input in the range would hide.
fields.explanation: Bugs cluster where the answer changes, so exactly min and exactly max are the values that expose a bound written one step off (min + 1, max - 1); a value inside the range is what catches a comparison made against the wrong bound. One below and one above exercise both clamping branches, and a hundred random values mostly retest the middle. "Only values that have caused bugs before" cannot cover the bug that has not happened yet.

problems: explanation claims exactly min and exactly max expose 'a comparison against the wrong bound', which is false: with min 0 and max 10, v < max ? min : v > max ? max : v agrees with a correct clamp at -1, 0, 10 and 11 and only differs at the inside values 1, 5 and 9
hint prescribes the key's own strategy ('test on both sides of that point'), which is the list option 1 gives
evidence: node: clamp probes at v = -1,0,1,5,9,10,11 (min 0, max 10) — correct 0,0,1,5,9,10,10; '<' swapped for '<=' identical (0,0,1,5,9,10,10); Math.min(Math.max(v,min+1),max-1) = 1,1,1,5,9,9,9, differing at exactly min and exactly max

notes: Reviewer was right that the '<' for '<=' swap is unobservable for clamp, but the replacement clause misassigns the wrong-bound bug to the boundary values; corrected to the inside value.
